questions.stem: About how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
options: 3 × 10⁸ km/s
questions.explanation: Light travels at about 300 000 km/s, which is 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Writing the same number with km/s makes it a thousand times too fast, and 340 m/s is the speed of sound in air — about a million times slower than light, which is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

questions.stem: Which of these is a luminous object?
options: A bike reflector
A candle flame
The full Moon
A bathroom mirror
questions.explanation: A luminous object gives off its own light, as a flame does. The Moon, a mirror and a bike reflector can all look bright, but they are non-luminous: we see them only because they reflect light from another source.

questions.stem: Frosted glass in a bathroom window lets light through but you cannot see clearly through it. The glass is:
options: luminous
translucent
transparent
opaque
questions.explanation: Translucent materials let light through but scatter it, so images are blurred. Transparent materials such as clear glass let light through without scattering, and opaque materials block light completely.

questions.stem: Which statement is the law of reflection?
options: The angle of reflection equals 90° minus the angle of incidence, from the normal
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal
The angle of reflection is always twice the angle of incidence, measured from the normal
Light always reflects straight back along the same path it arrived on
questions.explanation: Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle as it arrives, and both angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the surface. Light only reflects straight back along its own path when it hits the mirror along the normal, at an angle of incidence of zero.

questions.stem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at 30° to the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: Angles in the law of reflection are measured from the normal, not from the surface. A ray at 30° to the surface is at 90° − 30° = 60° to the normal, so the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are both 60°. Answering 30° uses the angle to the surface by mistake.

questions.stem: You stand 2 m in front of a flat bathroom mirror. Where does your image appear to be?
options: 4 m behind the mirror
On the surface of the mirror
1 m behind the mirror
2 m behind the mirror
questions.explanation: A plane mirror forms an image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so your image is 2 m behind it. The image is therefore 4 m from you, which is where the tempting 4 m comes from — but that is the distance from you, not from the mirror. The image is virtual: light only appears to come from behind the mirror, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

questions.stem: Why is the word AMBULANCE often printed back to front on the bonnet of an ambulance?
options: A rear-view mirror swaps left and right, so drivers ahead read it the right way
A rear-view mirror turns images upside down, so the letters must be flipped over
A rear-view mirror makes writing smaller unless the letters are reversed
The word is meant to be read by people standing behind the ambulance
questions.explanation: A plane mirror image is laterally inverted, so reversed writing appears the right way round in a driver's rear-view mirror. Plane mirrors do not turn images upside down or change their size — the image is upright and the same size as the object.

questions.stem: Shops and blind driveways often use curved convex mirrors. Why?
options: They bring light to a focus, making objects look larger and closer
They send light straight back to its source like a road reflector
They turn the image upside down so that movement is easier to spot
They spread out the reflected light, giving a wide field of view
questions.explanation: A convex mirror bulges outwards and spreads reflected rays apart, so it shows a wide area in one small mirror. The images are upright but smaller, so objects look further away than they are. Bringing light to a focus and magnifying is what a concave mirror does.

questions.stem: Which type of mirror is used behind the globe in a torch to send out a strong, narrow beam?
options: A plane mirror
A two-way mirror
A concave mirror
A convex mirror
questions.explanation: A concave mirror curves inwards; with the globe placed at its focal point, the reflected rays travel out parallel in a beam. A convex mirror does the opposite and spreads light out, which is useful for a wide view but not for a beam.

questions.stem: A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. Why?
options: Water pressure pushes on the light rays and bends them towards the base
Light changes speed and direction as it passes from water into air
The water's surface acts as a mirror and reflects part of the pencil
Light speeds up as it enters the water, so the rays curve downwards
questions.explanation: This is refraction: light changes speed when it crosses the boundary between water and air, and if it crosses at an angle it changes direction too. Light actually slows down in water, about a quarter slower than in air, so saying it speeds up gets the cause backwards.

questions.stem: A ray of light passes at an angle from air into a glass block. Which way does it bend, and why?
options: Away from the normal, because it slows down in the glass
Towards the normal, because it speeds up in the glass
It does not bend at all, because glass is transparent
Towards the normal, because it slows down in the glass
questions.explanation: Light slows down in a denser medium such as glass and bends towards the normal as it enters. When it leaves the glass it speeds up again and bends away from the normal. Transparent materials refract light too — that is how lenses work.

questions.stem: Why does a swimming pool look shallower than it really is?
options: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water
Light from the bottom bends towards the normal as it leaves the water's surface
The water's surface reflects the sky and hides the deepest parts
Blue water absorbs red light, which makes the floor look closer
questions.explanation: Light from the pool floor speeds up as it leaves the water and bends away from the normal. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays back to a point higher than the real floor. Light only bends towards the normal when it slows down, entering a denser medium.

questions.stem: Which type of lens brings parallel rays of light together at a focal point?
options: A sheet of frosted glass
A convex (converging) lens
A concave (diverging) lens
A flat sheet of clear glass
questions.explanation: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and refracts rays inwards so they meet at the focal point; a magnifying glass is a convex lens. A concave lens is thinner in the middle and spreads rays apart, so they never meet.

questions.stem: A short-sighted person sees nearby objects clearly, but distant objects look blurred. Which lens corrects this?
options: A convex lens, which spreads the light out before it enters the eye
A concave lens, which spreads the light out before it enters the eye
A convex lens, which brings the light together before it enters the eye
A concave lens, which brings the light together before it enters the eye
questions.explanation: In a short-sighted eye, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens spreads the rays slightly to move the focus back onto it. Long-sightedness is the opposite problem, focusing behind the retina, and is corrected with a converging convex lens.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye contains the light-sensitive cells that send signals to the brain?
options: The iris
The lens
The retina
The cornea
questions.explanation: The retina at the back of the eye is lined with rods and cones that turn light into nerve impulses. The cornea and lens refract light to focus it on the retina, and the iris controls how much light enters, but none of them detects light.

questions.stem: White light shone through a glass prism spreads out into a band of colours. Why?
options: The prism absorbs the white light and gives off new coloured light instead
Each colour reflects off a different face of the prism and leaves it separately
Each colour slows by a different amount, so each refracts at a different angle
The prism adds colours to the white light as it passes through the glass
questions.explanation: White light is already a mixture of colours. In glass, violet light slows the most and bends the most, while red slows the least and bends the least, so the colours separate — this is called dispersion. The prism does not create the colours; mixing them back together with a second prism gives white light again.

questions.stem: A red T-shirt is lit only by pure blue light in a dark room. What colour does it look?
options: Purple
Black
Red
Blue
questions.explanation: A red T-shirt looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the other colours. Pure blue light contains no red for it to reflect, so it absorbs the blue and looks black. The T-shirt cannot reflect a colour that is not shining on it.

questions.stem: Light signals travel along a curving optical fibre without escaping through the sides. What keeps the light inside?
options: The glass absorbing the light and giving it off again
Total internal reflection at the edge of the glass core
A silver mirror coating painted on the outside of the fibre
Diffraction that steers the light around each bend
questions.explanation: Light inside the core strikes its edge at an angle greater than the critical angle, so all of it is reflected back in and none refracts out. No mirror coating is needed. Absorption would weaken the signal, which is the opposite of what a fibre is designed to do.

questions.stem: Why is the daytime sky blue?
options: The sky reflects the blue colour of the oceans below it
The air absorbs every colour of sunlight except blue
Sunlight is made mostly of blue light before it reaches our atmosphere
Air molecules scatter blue light far more than red light
questions.explanation: Sunlight contains all colours, and tiny air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths such as blue much more strongly than red, so blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. The sky is blue far inland, away from any ocean, so reflection from the sea cannot be the cause.

questions.stem: In the particle model of light, light is made of:
options: sound vibrations too fast for us to hear
photons, which are small packets of energy
electrons travelling at very high speeds from the source
tiny atoms of glowing gas from the source
questions.explanation: In the particle model, light is a stream of photons, each carrying a small packet of energy. Scientists use both a wave model and a particle model of light, because each explains different behaviour. Electrons are particles of matter with mass and charge, which photons do not have.
